Critics argue that Persky’s ruling reflects a broader systemic issue of protecting privileged individuals. Supporters of the judge, however, claim the recall undermines judicial independence. If successful, this would be the first judicial recall in California in over 80 years, marking a significant moment in the state’s legal history.

Entrants to the annual event have five minutes to tell the biggest and most convincing lie they can. Winner George Kemp from Maryport, Cumbria was surprised to win as he initially thought his story about wrestling a bear in the Lake District was “too far-fetched.” The World’s Biggest Liar competition, held in Santon Bridge, Cumbria, drew participants from across the UK, each spinning wild tales to impress the judges. George’s dramatic recounting of his supposed bear encounter, complete with vivid details of claw marks and a daring escape, clinched the title. “I just made it up on the spot,” George admitted, laughing. “I never expected anyone to believe me!” The event, rooted in local folklore, celebrates the art of storytelling and humor. Organizers praised George’s creativity, noting his ability to keep the audience captivated. The competition continues to grow, attracting liars and laughter in equal measure each year.

The investigation found that only 28% of Welsh speakers had used the language with their GPs, dentists and opticians. Ms Huws said she hoped her report was the "beginning of a broader conversation about ensuring linguistic rights in healthcare settings." Her findings, published this week, highlight significant barriers faced by Welsh speakers in accessing services in their native tongue, despite legal protections under the Welsh Language Act.

The report surveyed over 1,000 individuals across Wales, revealing that many felt uncomfortable or unable to request services in Welsh due to a lack of bilingual staff or signage. Ms Huws emphasized the importance of cultural identity in healthcare, urging providers to prioritize language training and resources. She called for stronger enforcement of existing policies to ensure equal access. Health boards have pledged to review the findings and improve provisions for Welsh-speaking patients in the coming months.

The bill aims to revoke parts of the UK government's 2016 Trade Union Act. It would mean current restrictions on industrial action in the NHS, the fire service, schools, and other key sectors could be lifted, allowing workers greater freedom to strike. The 2016 legislation imposed strict thresholds for strike ballots, requiring a minimum 50% turnout and, in essential services, support from at least 40% of eligible voters. Critics argue these rules have curtailed workers’ rights and hindered their ability to negotiate better pay and conditions.

Supporters of the new bill, including trade unions, claim it will restore balance in labor relations, empowering employees to advocate for fair treatment. However, opponents warn that easing restrictions could lead to increased disruption in critical public services. The proposal has sparked heated debate in Parliament, with the government set to review its broader implications on the economy and public safety.

Evha Jannath, 11, was on a school trip on Tuesday when she fell from a circular boat on Splash Canyon at Drayton Manor. Alton Towers and Legoland Windsor are among the theme parks expressing their condolences following the tragic incident. Evha, a student from Leicester, was visiting the Staffordshire park with her school group when the accident occurred. Despite immediate efforts by park staff and emergency services to rescue her from the water, she was pronounced dead at the scene.

Drayton Manor has temporarily closed the ride for a thorough investigation, and the park issued a statement expressing deep sorrow over the loss. Authorities are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the fall. The incident has sparked renewed discussions on theme park safety protocols. Evha’s family described her as a bright and cheerful child, and the community mourns her untimely passing. Further updates are awaited as investigations continue.

An early own goal from Ally Gilchrist and a thunderous strike from James Tavernier put the Championship winners into an unassailable lead. Andy Halliday added a penalty and Kenny Miller sealed the rout with a clinical finish, ensuring a commanding 4-0 victory for Rangers over their rivals at Ibrox Stadium. The match, which showcased Rangers' dominance from the opening whistle, left little doubt about their superiority in the league this season. Gilchrist’s unfortunate error in the fifth minute set the tone, while Tavernier’s long-range effort in the 20th minute electrified the crowd. Halliday converted from the spot just before halftime, and Miller’s goal in the second half capped a perfect day for the home side. Manager Mark Warburton praised his team’s relentless attacking play, stating, “We were clinical and focused throughout.” This result further cements Rangers’ position at the top, as they continue their march towards an unbeaten run.

Members of the Royal College of Midwives (RCM) intend to stop work for four hours. They voted by 9-1 in favour of strike action - the first such vote in the organization’s 140-year history. This unprecedented decision comes amid growing concerns over pay, working conditions, and chronic staff shortages in maternity services across the UK. The RCM, representing over 50,000 midwives and support workers, has warned that the current situation is unsustainable, with many members feeling undervalued and overworked.

The planned four-hour strike aims to send a strong message to the government, urging immediate action to address these issues. RCM leaders have emphasized that patient safety remains a priority, with emergency care provisions in place during the strike. Negotiations with health authorities are ongoing, but without significant improvements, further industrial action could follow. This historic vote highlights the deepening crisis in the UK’s maternity care system.

The number given for the current account customers hit by the fraud is fewer than half of the 20,000 initially reported to have been affected. Personal data "was not compromised," according to a statement from the bank, which has been working to address the issue swiftly. The fraud, which involved unauthorized transactions, was first detected last month, prompting an internal investigation and immediate action to secure accounts.

The bank clarified that fewer than 10,000 customers were actually impacted, and affected individuals have been contacted with steps to recover any losses. Authorities are collaborating with the institution to trace the source of the fraud, believed to be linked to a sophisticated phishing scheme. Customers are urged to remain vigilant and report any suspicious activity. The bank has also rolled out enhanced security measures to prevent future incidents, reassuring clients of their commitment to safeguarding finances.

Construction workers are required to hold a CSCS card to prove skills and a knowledge of health and safety. But a joint BBC London/Newsnight investigation found organised cheating. Carl Rhymer, a whistleblower from the construction industry, revealed that some training centres are helping workers bypass the necessary tests by providing answers or even taking exams on their behalf. This fraudulent practice undermines the integrity of the CSCS scheme, which is designed to ensure safety on building sites.

The investigation uncovered that certain centres charge exorbitant fees for guaranteed passes, exploiting workers desperate to secure employment. This poses serious risks, as unqualified individuals may lack the critical safety knowledge needed to prevent accidents. Industry leaders have called for stricter oversight and penalties for offending centres. The Construction Skills Certification Scheme has pledged to investigate and revoke cards obtained fraudulently, but critics argue that systemic flaws must be addressed to restore trust.

The hackers have made a ransom demand of 100 Bitcoin, which amounts to about $70,000 (£56,000; €66,000). As a precaution, staff shut off all ticketing machines on the network to prevent further breaches after a cyberattack targeted the public transport system late last night. Authorities confirmed that the attack compromised sensitive data, potentially exposing passenger information. 

The transport authority issued a statement urging commuters to use alternative payment methods while technicians work to secure the system. Cybersecurity experts have been deployed to investigate the breach and identify the source of the attack. Meanwhile, passengers expressed frustration over the disruption, with many unable to purchase tickets during the morning rush. 

Officials have not yet decided whether to pay the ransom, citing concerns over encouraging future attacks. The incident highlights the growing threat of ransomware targeting critical infrastructure, prompting calls for stronger digital defenses across public services.

The British pair were beaten by Moreno de Pauw and Kenny de Ketele of Belgium in the final race, the madison. Wiggins, 36, plans to retire after the Six Day event, marking the end of an illustrious career that includes five Olympic gold medals and a historic Tour de France victory in 2012. Partnered with Mark Cavendish, Wiggins aimed to cap his journey with a win at the London Six Day, but the Belgian duo proved too strong, securing victory with superior tactics and endurance. Despite the defeat, Wiggins expressed pride in his performance and gratitude to the fans who cheered him on throughout the event. Cavendish, a long-time teammate, praised Wiggins’ dedication, calling him an inspiration to British cycling. As Wiggins prepares to hang up his helmet, the cycling world reflects on his remarkable legacy, celebrating a career that redefined the sport for a generation.

The Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) report said cockpit footage showed the plane "responding to the pilot's control inputs". It also said pilot Andy Hill was thrown clear of the aircraft during a tragic incident at the Shoreham Airshow in 2015. The crash, involving a vintage Hawker Hunter jet, resulted in the deaths of 11 people on the ground and left several others injured. The report highlighted that the aircraft was performing a maneuver at a dangerously low altitude, failing to achieve the necessary height to complete the loop safely. Despite the plane responding to Hill’s commands, the combination of speed and altitude proved fatal. Hill survived the crash but sustained serious injuries. The AAIB emphasized that the tragedy underscored the critical need for stringent safety protocols at airshows. Investigations into contributing factors, including pilot error and event planning, have sparked debates over regulations to prevent future disasters of this nature.

An area of land stretching from Bo'ness Harbour to the former Kinneil colliery is to become a haven for wildlife and plants. It is the second Local Nature Reserve created in the Falkirk Council area, following years of planning and community consultation. The Kinneil Foreshore, spanning over 100 hectares, will be transformed into a protected space to support biodiversity and provide a natural retreat for locals and visitors alike.

The reserve will feature restored habitats for native species, including birds, insects, and rare plants, with walking trails and interpretive signage to educate the public on the area's ecological importance. Local environmental groups have hailed the decision as a significant step towards conservation, while council officials emphasize the balance between nature preservation and public access. Work on the reserve is set to begin next spring, with hopes it will inspire similar projects across the region.

Spencer Flower claimed his involvement with a social housing company was not relevant to a debate in 2013 over the future of housing in east Dorset. But he was found to have potentially misled the public, as his ties to the company raised questions about a conflict of interest. Flower, a prominent local councillor at the time, insisted his position did not influence his stance during discussions on housing policies. However, an investigation revealed that his undisclosed connection could have swayed decisions benefiting the company. Critics argued this lack of transparency undermined trust in local governance. The controversy sparked a broader debate on ethical standards for public officials, with calls for stricter disclosure rules. Flower later issued a statement expressing regret for any perceived impropriety, though he maintained his actions were in good faith. The incident remains a cautionary tale about accountability in local politics.

Black, who died in 2015, had a UK top 10 hit in 1964 with It's for You, written by McCartney and John Lennon. McCartney recorded his own version earlier that year, but it was Cilla Black’s emotive rendition that captured the hearts of British audiences, peaking at number 7 on the charts. The song, a heartfelt ballad, showcased Black’s powerful voice and cemented her status as a prominent figure in the 1960s music scene. Managed by Brian Epstein, who also guided The Beatles, Black became a household name with a string of hits during that era. McCartney and Lennon, known for their prolific songwriting, tailored the track specifically for her, highlighting their versatility beyond rock and roll. Black’s success with It's for You remains a testament to her talent and the enduring magic of The Beatles’ songwriting, a collaboration that defined a golden age of British pop music.

He started the project after growing frustrated about the number of options and amount of recorded information on call centre menus. Mr Clarke discovered that some automated menus have nearly 50 different prompts, often leaving callers confused and irritated. Determined to simplify the process, he launched an innovative app called "MenuMapper," designed to help users navigate complex phone systems with ease.

The app, which has already gained thousands of downloads, allows users to search for specific companies and instantly access a visual map of their call centre menus. This eliminates the need to listen through lengthy recordings or press countless buttons. Mr Clarke, a former IT specialist, spent over a year researching and compiling data from hundreds of companies to ensure accuracy. "I wanted to save people time and frustration," he said. Industry experts have praised MenuMapper as a game-changer, predicting it could revolutionize customer service interactions worldwide.

Envoy Sigrid Kaag was speaking as Syria appeared to miss a Sunday deadline to remove its arsenal from the country. All Syria's chemical weapons are scheduled to be destroyed by June 30 under an international agreement brokered to prevent further use of such weapons in the ongoing civil war. Kaag, the UN-OPCW joint mission coordinator, expressed concern over the delay, noting that only a fraction of the declared stockpile has been shipped out for destruction. She urged the Syrian government to expedite the process to meet the critical deadline, emphasizing the importance of eliminating these weapons to ensure civilian safety. The international community, including the United States and Russia, has been closely monitoring the situation, with growing frustration over Syria's slow compliance. Failure to adhere to the timeline could lead to renewed calls for stricter measures or sanctions against the Assad regime, further complicating the conflict.
